open-question.question: Most of the 35 invariants in today's `CLAUDE.md` govern files under `core/` (the six tools, the shared procedures, the skills, the agents), yet `core/` can hold no node: the host build stops on any file at its top level and renders every file under its four directories into every host tree, and a standing rule keeps editor-facing prose and rationale out of those rendered files, tool sources included. The goal has the parent node, the small root, describe `core/`. Where do the compressed rules governing files under `core/` live: in the root itself, in a file outside `core/` that the root points at, inside the governed files with the rule against rationale in runtime files lifted in whole or for the tool sources only, or in a file under `core/` that the build is changed to leave unrendered?

Some of today's invariants govern files in more than one folder, for example the slot rule (`core/` and `scripts/hosts/`), the fixed console lines (the skills under `core/`, the table in `docs/skill-reference.md`, its test under `tests/`, and the extension's build), and each tool with its tests. The mission places each compressed rule where someone working there will find it. Where does a rule spanning several folders live: once in the node of the folder holding what it chiefly governs with a pointer from each other folder's node, once in the nearest node above all of them, or restated in every node it touches?
open-question.alternative: The whole compressed rule (its rule, its reason, and its retired forms) is stated once, in the node of the folder holding what it chiefly governs, and every other touched folder's node carries a pointer to it with a when-to-follow note. This applies to every spanning rule, as one project-wide rule written into the root's rules on where knowledge lives: the slot rule in the node covering `core/` or `scripts/hosts/`, the fixed console lines in the one covering the skills or the table, each tool's rule where the tool is described and a pointer from `tests/`. The rule has one text that cannot drift, it sits beside the files a change to it usually starts from, and every other place it binds still leads there through a pointer the pytest check proves resolves, so the root stays small. Someone must judge which folder a rule chiefly governs, and for rules with no dominant folder (the fixed console lines spread over `core/`, `docs/`, `tests/`, and `gurita-vscode/`) the choice is arbitrary. A reader in a pointing folder gets only a note until they follow the pointer. Where the chief folder is `core/` the home depends on where the Home of core rules question puts rules governing `core/`, and how a pointer can name a place inside a node depends on the Pointer form question.

alternative.id: Nearest common node by read path

open-question.alternative: The whole compressed rule is stated once, in the nearest node above every folder it touches, and the touched folders' nodes carry no pointer to it. A reader is expected to find it because the root's rules on how nodes are read have every reader read each node on the path from the root down to the folder they work in. Placement needs no judgment, since the common ancestor is fixed by the folders alone, and no pointer is added or kept, so each rule costs its bytes once and nothing else. Almost every spanning rule named here (the slot rule, the fixed console lines, a tool with its tests) touches more than one top-level folder, so its nearest common node is the root, which the goal requires to be small and which the earlier hand compression saw grow back to 172 KB. It also works only for readers who actually read the whole path; a runner that enters a deep node through one pointer never sees the rule. Its fit with the root's limit depends on the Byte budget values question.

The whole compressed rule is stated once, in the nearest node above every folder it touches, and each touched folder's node also carries a pointer up to it with a when-to-follow note. Placement still needs no judgment of which folder matters most, and a reader who enters any touched folder's node directly, without reading the path above it, is still led to the rule. The rules still collect in the root for the same reason, now with pointers added below, so the root's budget is spent on cross-folder rules beside the pointers, the bootstrap section, and the rules that bind everywhere; most of the root's growth risk returns. Its fit depends on the Byte budget values question.

One stated test, written into the root's rules on where knowledge lives, picks each spanning rule's single home: the node of the folder holding most of what it governs when one folder clearly does, and the nearest common node above them otherwise; in both cases every other touched folder's node carries a pointer to the home with a when-to-follow note. Rules with a clear centre of gravity sit beside that centre and keep the root small, while rules with none still get a home fixed by a stated test rather than an arbitrary pick. Two placements coexist and a reader cannot tell from a rule's subject which one it took without applying the test, and the "clearly" in the test is itself a judgment that two runners may make differently. Rules that fall to the common node still land mostly in the root, within whatever the Byte budget values question allows.

The whole compressed rule (rule, reason, retired forms) is stated once, in the node of the folder it chiefly governs; every other touched folder's node states the rule's binding sentence itself in one line, without its reason or retired forms, followed by a pointer to the full home. A reader working in any touched folder sees what binds them there without following anything, while the reason and the retired forms, the bulk of each rule, still have one home. The binding sentence exists in several places, and no check can prove the copies still say what the home says, so a later change to the rule can leave a stale one-liner that contradicts it. It shares the chief-folder judgment of the pointer-only form, and each copy spends a node's byte budget.

A spanning rule is broken into the parts that bind in each folder, each part stated, with its reason and retired forms, in its own folder's node (for the fixed console lines: the skills' rule for printing lines where the skills are described, the table's rule in `docs/`, the test's rule in `tests/`), and the parts point at one another so the coupling between them is still visible. Each node holds only rules that bind in its own folder, with nothing restated and no folder chosen as the chief one, so a reader anywhere gets the full local obligation where they work. Many spanning rules are about the coupling itself (the table and its test changing together, a tool and its tests, a slot used in `core/` and declared under `scripts/hosts/`), and splitting them scatters the one reason that justifies all the parts, so the reason is either repeated in each part or held by none. The cross-pointers between parts multiply with the number of folders.

The whole compressed rule, its rule, reason, and retired forms, is restated in the node of every folder it touches, with no single home and no pointer between the copies. Each reader finds the complete rule, reason included, in the one node they read for the folder they work in, with no pointer to follow and no node to judge as the chief one. Every copy can drift from the others and the pytest check cannot detect it, so the tree carries the same drift the 172 KB file accumulated, now spread over several nodes; each copy also spends a node's byte budget, so the most widely spanning rules cost the most where the budget is tightest.

Every rule spanning several folders is stated once, in one dedicated document outside the node tree for cross-folder rules, which the root points at, and each touched folder's node carries a pointer to the rule's place in that document with a when-to-follow note. The root stays small and no rule needs a chief folder or a common node picked for it, while the cross-folder rules, the ones most likely to be changed from more than one place, are all read together. It brings back a central rules file of the kind the goal retires, the place the 172 KB file's growth came from, now bounded only by whatever budget it gets, and the rule sits next to none of the files it governs. Whether such a file overlaps the one the Home of core rules question may create for rules governing `core/` depends on that question.

The project states no rule for where a spanning rule lives: each spanning rule's home, and whether it is pointed at or restated, is chosen for that rule alone when it is placed, with the pytest check enforcing only that whatever pointers exist resolve. Each rule can be placed where it actually reads best, without bending rules of very different shapes (a coupling between a table and its test, a tool and its tests, a slot convention) to one placement form. Nothing tells a later editor or the update skill where to look for, or where to put, a new spanning rule, so the tree drifts toward inconsistent placements over time. Whether each rule's home is still fixed now depends on the Placement decision timing question, which decides whether a map from item to home is recorded before tasks or left to each task's runner.

open-question.question: The mission re-evaluates every one of the 35 invariants in today's `CLAUDE.md` and compresses each to its rule, its reason, and the retired forms that must not return. May a re-evaluation end in a rule itself being dropped or changed, for example one found obsolete or one that only records an accepted limitation, or does the mission change only wording and placement, every rule standing exactly as it binds today?
open-question.alternative: No rule is dropped or changed: every one of the 35 invariants keeps binding exactly as it does today. Re-evaluation cuts only text that binds nothing (mechanics already stated in the runtime files, field measurements, dates, the history of how a form came about) and moves each rule to its home. An entry that records an accepted limitation ("accepted as it stands", "accepted as never to be changed") stays as a rule, compressed to what must not be changed and why. Candidates for retirement are not recorded anywhere. The mission's diff can be reviewed as a pure move and compression: no tool, test, runtime file, or behaviour changes, and a reviewer has only to check that every rule survives, so the risk of losing a design decision while rewriting 145,667 bytes is the lowest of any option. Rules whose subject no longer stands in the tree (the pre-split missions, the pre-flip TASKS_DONE.md note) and entries kept only to stop a limitation being "fixed" are carried into the new tree as they are, so part of the bulk the byte budgets must hold is text the re-evaluation already judged dead, and the goal's "every invariant is re-evaluated" yields nothing beyond compression.

alternative.id: Wording only, candidates kept for later

open-question.alternative: This mission changes only wording and placement, every rule binding as it does today, as in the wording-only option. Where re-evaluation finds a rule obsolete or one that only records an accepted limitation, the runner leaves the rule standing in its new home and records it as a retirement candidate, with the reason, in one draft under ideas/ for a later mission to decide. Keeps this mission's diff a pure move and compression while not wasting the judgment the re-evaluation forms: the candidates reach a later mission as a ready list, where each drop can be decided on its own with the tree already in place. The dead text still has to fit inside this mission's byte budgets, and the draft is one more document the tree must point at and the update skill must keep honest until a later mission takes it up, which nothing schedules.

alternative.id: Drop obsolete rules, decided up front

open-question.alternative: A rule may be dropped, never changed, and only when its subject no longer exists in the tree or the history it guards is closed (for example the pre-split missions and the pre-flip TASKS_DONE.md note); every other rule, accepted-limitation entries included, keeps binding exactly as today. Each drop is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, the review pass authoring one open question per candidate, so the recorded decisions list every rule that leaves. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Removes the clearest dead weight from the tree while every drop is a recorded, revertible decision rather than a runner's call, and the rule that stops a limitation being "fixed" is left untouched, so no behaviour can drift. Adds a round of questions before derivation for a handful of small drops, and an obsolete-looking rule may still bind something (the TASKS_DONE.md note also says no runner is to read or recreate the file), so each candidate needs care that a compressed retired-forms line could have given at no cost.

alternative.id: Drop obsolete and limitation rules, decided up front

open-question.alternative: A rule may be dropped, never changed, when it is obsolete or when it only records an accepted limitation (the commit tool's exit-128 retry accepted as it stands, the hand-rendered attribute rule, markup accepted in an alternative's text, the unbounded show print); a dropped limitation entry leaves behaviour as it is and stops forbidding a later fix. Each drop is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per candidate. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Cuts the largest class of text that binds no current behaviour, the accepted-limitation records written in the latest mission's tasks, so the tree states what the code must do rather than every fix that was weighed and declined. An accepted-limitation entry exists precisely so a later editor does not "fix" what was left on purpose; dropping it removes that guard, and a later mission may re-measure and re-decide something already settled, at a cost the drop saved only in bytes.

A rule may be dropped, never changed, when its subject no longer exists in the tree, under one criterion recorded as a decision of this mission; the task runner compressing that area applies it and names each dropped rule, with its reason, in its task's verified bar. Accepted-limitation entries and every other rule keep binding as today. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Removes dead rules without a question round before derivation, since applying one narrow, checkable criterion (the subject is gone from the tree) is a runner's job, and every drop still shows in a commit body and its diff. A design decision leaves the project's record by a runner's judgment rather than a recorded answer, and a runner reading "subject gone" loosely can drop a rule that still binds (a retired form that must not return is exactly a rule whose subject is gone); how much is left to runners also depends on the axis the Placement decision timing question owns.

alternative.id: Drop or change rules, docs only

open-question.alternative: Re-evaluation may drop a rule (obsolete or limitation-only) or change what it binds, narrowing, loosening, or merging rules where it finds one wrong or redundant, but only where the change needs no edit to a runtime file, tool, test, or build: the rules change what a later editor may do, never what the code does now. Each drop or change is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per rule. Gives the re-evaluation its full value at the level of the rules themselves, so overlapping or contradictory invariants written over many missions can be reconciled into a smaller, coherent set rather than faithfully compressed, while the plugin's behaviour stays exactly as shipped. Many questions may be raised across 35 rules before derivation, lengthening the mission's preparation, and a rule changed without touching the code it governs can leave code that the new rule no longer explains or that now contradicts it until a later mission aligns them.

alternative.id: Drop or change rules with the code

open-question.alternative: Re-evaluation may drop or change any rule, and a changed rule carries the change to the runtime files, tools, tests, and rebuilt host trees it governs in this mission, so rule and code stay in step. Each drop or change is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per rule. Every rule in the new tree states exactly what the code does, with no rule left wrong or out of step, and a defect the re-evaluation exposes is fixed where it is found rather than deferred. Turns a documentation mission into a plugin-behaviour mission of unbounded size across all of core/ and the host trees, overlapping the defined mission_project-defined-knowledge-placement/ that changes the context-reading runners and finish, and mixes behaviour changes into a diff that is otherwise reviewable as moves and compression.

open-question.question: The mission gives each of the 35 invariants in today's `CLAUDE.md` a new home and a compressed text, and gives the other sections of that file (commands, repository layout, the skill pipeline, mission file structure, development notes) new homes as well. Is each item's home settled in this mission's recorded decisions before tasks are derived, as a map from item to destination, or is it left to the runner completing each task, judged under the recorded placement rules?
open-question.alternative: Before tasks are derived, the mission's recorded decisions hold a complete map. Each of the 35 invariants and each of the other sections of today's `CLAUDE.md` (commands, repository layout, the skill pipeline, mission file structure, development notes, what the repo is) is assigned its destination: the root, a named `README.md` node, a description in a parent node, or another named document. Review passes author the map, and the answering skills settle it. Task derivation reads the map as given, and each completing runner places what the map assigns it with no placement judgment of its own. Every home is reviewed and recorded once, against the whole file and every other home, before any text moves. A misplaced rule then shows up as an open question during preparation, where it costs one answer, instead of as a task commit to revert. The map also becomes the as-of record that later readers and the update skill can check the tree against. It adds the most preparation work. About forty item-level placements must be written up as questions or as one large map decision and then answered, and `## Decisions` swells with a table that is spent once the tree exists. A home also gets fixed before anyone has written the compressed text, and it is the compressed text that may show where a rule really belongs. How heavy the map is depends on how much the placement rules settled by the sibling questions (Home of core rules, Rules spanning folders, Root-level file entries) already decide on their own.

Before tasks are derived, the recorded decisions settle the homes only of the items the recorded placement rules leave open or ambiguous. A review pass names these items once it has read the rules against the 35 invariants and the other sections: for example a rule governing files in several folders, a rule about `core/`, or a section with no obvious single folder. Every other item goes to the runner completing its task, who places it under the recorded rules. The human review is spent only where placement is a real judgment. The mechanical cases, such as a tool invariant going to the node of the folder that holds its tool and tests, cost no question. Preparation stays proportionate, and the hard cases are still settled before execution. Which items count as contested is itself a judgment made in review, and an item it misses reaches a runner as if it were mechanical. The record is split: some homes are in `## Decisions`, and the rest show only in task commit diffs. How many items end up contested depends on how much the sibling placement-rule questions settle.

No item-level placement is recorded as a decision. The `derive-tasks` run that decomposes the mission applies the recorded placement rules to every item in one pass and writes each item's destination into the briefs. Tasks are cut per destination node or per group of items, and each brief names the items its task moves and where they go. Completing runners follow the briefs. One runner decides every home in one sitting, against the whole file. The map is therefore consistent and complete without one review question per item, and the task list itself becomes the map, ordered by dependency. Task derivation is meant to decompose recorded decisions, not to make new ones. Here about forty placement judgments are made at the one step no review pass or answer looks at. Briefs of one to three sentences can barely list the items and destinations of a whole node, so a placement error is found only when a task lands.

No item-level placement is recorded before derivation. The derived list opens with a task that reads today's `CLAUDE.md` against the recorded placement rules and decides every item's home. That task records its map by rewriting the queued later tasks' briefs through the completion procedure's queued-task revision step (the task-list tool's `replace`), so the map rides in its own `Task-completion:` commit. The later placing tasks follow their rewritten briefs. A single judgment covers every home, so the map stays consistent across nodes. It is made by an execution runner, which reads the live file in full and is allowed to explore. It needs neither review questions per item nor new decisions at derivation, and the whole map lands in one reviewable commit before any text moves. The map is never reviewed as an open question. A person sees it only in a commit, after it has already steered every later brief, and an unattended run carries on from it. It also makes derivation guess the shape of the later tasks before their contents are known, and it relies on the rewritten briefs fitting their length limit.

No map exists anywhere. The recorded decisions hold only the placement rules, the briefs name which items each task works through (for example a group of invariants or one section of today's `CLAUDE.md`) without destinations, and the runner completing each task chooses each item's home under the recorded rules while it compresses the item. Preparation and derivation carry the least weight. Each home is chosen by the runner holding the item's compressed text and the live folder it might go into, which is the most information any decider will have about where that item fits. About forty placement judgments are spread over separate runners, which may be isolated agents, and none of them sees the others' choices. Similar rules can land in different kinds of homes, and a node may be written before a later task adds to it. The only check left is the pytest check, which tests pointers, coverage, and budgets, not whether a rule sits where someone working there will find it. How well this works depends on how precisely the sibling questions' placement rules decide a home on their own.

open-question.question: The goal fixes what the root `CLAUDE.md` holds but not what a `README.md` node below it holds. Does every node follow one fixed structure, and if so which parts does it have, for example the folder's purpose, the rules binding work there each with its reason and retired forms, the commands run there, an entry per file, and pointers to the nodes below, or is a node free prose bound only by its byte budget and the pointer form?
open-question.alternative: Every node, and every description a parent node gives a folder whose `README.md` name is taken or rendered (`core/`, `hosts/`, `gurita-vscode/`), has the same five parts in one fixed order under fixed headings: the folder's purpose; the rules binding work there, each one entry stating the rule, its reason, and its retired forms; the commands run there; one entry per file in the folder; and the pointers to the nodes below. Every part is present in every node, an empty one written as a fixed one-line placeholder. The pytest check verifies the headings and their order beside its pointer, covered-folder, and byte-budget checks. Every node reads the same way, so a runner or maintainer knows where the rules, commands, and files of any folder stand before opening it, and the check catches a missing or misplaced part as it catches a broken pointer. One entry per file brings back the growth that made today's layout block 14,023 bytes (its `tests/` entry alone 3,343), across folders of 86 (`tests/`) and 124 (`gurita-vscode/`) files, every new file becoming a node edit and placeholders spending bytes in small folders; it also adds a structure check the goal's list of three does not name. Whether full file inventories fit at all depends on the node limit the byte-budget sibling sets.

Every node, and every in-parent description of a taken or rendered folder, draws its sections from one closed, ordered list of parts: purpose (required), rules (each entry the rule, its reason, and its retired forms), commands, files (entries only for files that do not already document themselves in a docstring, `--help`, or header), and pointers to the nodes below. A part other than purpose appears only when the folder has something for it, always under its fixed heading and in the list's order, and no heading outside the list is allowed. The pytest check verifies the required part, the allowed headings, and their order. Keeps the predictable shape of a fixed template, checked mechanically, while a small folder such as `snippets/` or `.claude-plugin/` writes only the parts it needs and file entries stay limited to what no file already says of itself. Adds a structure check beyond the three the goal names, and judging which files document themselves is an author's call the check cannot verify, so the files part can still drift from the folder; heading rules also constrain how cross-folder rules and pointers are written, which the rules-spanning-folders and pointer-form siblings decide.

The same closed, ordered list of parts as the checked variant (purpose required; rules with reason and retired forms, commands, files only for files that do not document themselves, and pointers below, each present only when held), applied to every node and every in-parent description, but stated only as a convention in the root's rules on where knowledge lives and how nodes are read, followed by node authors and the update skill. The pytest check stays at pointers, covered folders, and byte budgets. Gives every node a shared shape with no check beyond the three the goal names, so a node that needs a part the list lacks can be written without first changing a test. Nothing mechanical holds the shape, so it drifts the way the root file grew back after the 2026-09-23 compression, and its upkeep rests on the update skill, whose job the update-skill sibling decides.

Every node, and every in-parent description, has a fixed, ordered set of parts with no per-file part at all: purpose (required), rules (each the rule, its reason, and its retired forms), commands, and pointers to the nodes below, each part other than purpose present only when held. A file is known from listing the folder and from its own docstring, `--help`, or header; what a node says of a particular file is said inside a rule or the purpose. The pytest check verifies the allowed headings and their order. Removes the one part that grows with the file count and goes stale with every added or renamed file, so nodes stay within budget as folders grow and nothing restates what the files already say of themselves. A file that does not document itself (a fixture under `tests/fixtures/`, a media asset under `gurita-vscode/media/`, a drawing under `assets/`) gets no entry anywhere, so a newcomer must open it to learn its role; the structure check is still one beyond the goal's three.

Every node fixes only its navigational frame: a required opening statement of the folder's purpose and a required closing part holding the pointers to the nodes below (absent in a node with nothing below). Everything between, rules with their reasons and retired forms, commands, file notes, is free prose in whatever order the folder suits, bound by the byte budget and the pointer form. The pytest check verifies the two framing parts. Fixes exactly what traversal of the tree needs, where a node is about and where to go next, while leaving content shape to the folder, so a rule-heavy folder such as `tests/` and a one-file folder are both written naturally. A reader cannot know where in a node the binding rules stand or whether a node holds any, so a rule with its retired forms can be buried in prose and missed by someone about to restore a retired form.

No fixed structure: each node, and each in-parent description, is free prose bound only by its byte budget and the pointer form, its shape left to whoever writes it (the runner completing each node's task, later the update skill), with no rule on parts stated in the root and nothing checked beyond pointers, covered folders, and byte budgets. The cheapest to write and maintain and the closest to the goal as worded, whose check names only pointers, covered folders, and budgets; each node takes the shape its folder's knowledge actually has. Nodes written by different runners diverge in shape, so finding the rules or commands of a folder means reading its whole node, and with no shape to compare against, staleness and growth are visible only through the byte budget.

open-question.question: The mission's pytest check must find every pointer in the root `CLAUDE.md` and in each `README.md` node below it and prove that it resolves, and the eighteen places where today's invariants refer to one another by name become references between nodes. In what written form does a node point at another node, a file, or a place inside one, so that the check can tell a pointer from ordinary prose and resolve it: a relative Markdown link, a backticked repo-relative path, or a fixed list form of its own?

The mission's pytest check requires every covered folder to have a node, a `README.md` of its own or, where that name is taken or rendered, a description in its parent node. The repository tracks thirteen top-level folders, some holding one file (`.claude-plugin/`, `snippets/`), with subfolders below them such as `core/skills/<name>/`, `scripts/hosts/<host>/`, `tests/fixtures/`, and `gurita-vscode/src/`, beside the transient `mission_<slug>/` directories, the fixture trees, and the build output under `hosts/`. By what rule does a folder count as covered: every tracked top-level folder only, every tracked folder at any depth, every folder meeting a stated test such as a file count, or an explicit list kept by hand?

The mission's pytest check holds the root `CLAUDE.md`, every `README.md` node below it, and each pointer's when-to-follow note within a byte budget, and the three limits constrain one another, since the root carries one pointer with its note for each of the thirteen tracked top-level folders beside its other contents and a node carries the pointers to what lies below it. Today's root is 171,838 bytes, and an earlier hand compression to 22,329 bytes grew back. What are the three byte limits: for the root, for a node, and for a note?

The goal lists what the small root `CLAUDE.md` holds, among it one pointer per top-level folder, and names no place for what must be known about the files standing at the repository root, which today's layout block describes one entry each (`VERSION`, `task_line_rules.txt`, `answer_decision_principles.md`, the policy and contributor files). Where is that recorded: as entries in the root within its byte budget, in a document the root points at, only in each file's own header or in `CONTRIBUTING.md`, or nowhere beyond the rules that bind everywhere?

GitHub's documentation says a `README.md` in `.github/` is shown as the repository's front page ahead of the root one, which has not been checked against this repository, whose root `README.md` is the public landing page. Is `.github/` treated as a folder whose `README.md` name is taken, described by the root like `core/`, `hosts/`, and `gurita-vscode/`, or does it get a `README.md` node once that behaviour is checked and found not to apply?

The mission re-evaluates and streamlines `docs/`, four pages of 188,503 bytes: `skill-reference.md` (one entry per skill or dispatched agent and the fixed console lines table), `workflow.md`, `ways-of-using.md`, and `design-claims.md`, linked from the public root `README.md` and named by today's `CLAUDE.md` as a home of the mechanics its invariants leave out. Which reader does `docs/` serve once the node tree exists, and so what is cut: public documentation for the plugin's users only, with everything maintainer-facing moved to the nodes or dropped; maintainer reference beside the nodes; or both as today, shortened only where a page restates a runtime file?

The `## Fixed console lines` table of `docs/skill-reference.md`, 87 rows, is parsed at that path and heading by `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py` and by `gurita-vscode/scripts/bundle.js`, which writes its rows into the extension's bundled `fixed_lines.tsv` at build time. While the mission streamlines `docs/`, does the table stay at that path under that heading whatever happens to the rest of the page, or may it move, with both readers changed to follow it?

The mission adds a maintainer-only skill under `.claude/skills/` that, beside a pytest check of pointers, covered folders, and byte budgets, keeps the tree of `README.md` nodes below the root `CLAUDE.md` honest. What does one run of that skill do: repair only what the check reports, compare every node with the folder it describes and rewrite what has gone stale, bring the nodes up to date with the commits made since its last run, or re-compress nodes that have grown?

The plugin as it stands points its context-reading runners at the root context file alone and has `finish-mission` record a mission's lasting changes by editing and committing only that file. A second live mission, `mission_project-defined-knowledge-placement/`, defined but not started, would have those runners read whatever the context file directs them to and have finish write wherever it says such knowledge belongs; both missions stand at the root, so only one can execute at a time. Does this mission's tree assume that mission's changes have landed, or must it hold with the plugin as it stands, where a runner reaches a node only by following the root's own instructions and a later mission's lasting changes reach a node only through its tasks or the update skill?
open-question.alternative: The tree assumes nothing of `mission_project-defined-knowledge-placement/`. It works with the runners as they are: they read the root context file alone through the `CONTEXT_FILE` slot, and they reach a node only by following the root's own pointers and rules on how nodes are read. `finish-mission` keeps recording a mission's lasting changes in the root alone, and those changes reach a node only through a later mission's tasks or the maintainer-only update skill. Neither mission waits on the other. Whichever reaches task entry first takes the root scope, and the other follows. The design rests on behaviour that exists and can be checked today, not on a mission that has no starting state and no decisions yet.
